title: Will you ever be good?
hook: will you ever be simple, whole, unconcealed? (Meditations 10.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: pray differently. Your line was let me not fear. Where did you find the fear under a wish? Day six hundred thirteen.

A face for work. A face for family dinners. A face for the group chat. Each one fits. Each one can be a little tiring to wear. And underneath them all, someone is doing the switching. Book ten of the Meditations opens with Marcus asking himself that question, not as a theory, but in the second person, like someone gently shaking his own shoulder. Today, as book ten begins: contented disposition.
screen: `A FACE FOR EVERY ROOM.` → `WHO'S UNDERNEATH?` → `BOOK TEN OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the address. Marcus speaks to his own soul: will you ever, my soul, be good and simple and one and naked, plainer to see than the body that surrounds you? He isn't writing a rule. He's asking a question he doesn't know the answer to. Second, the words. Good. Simple: single, one fold, not doubled over. One: whole, not split into different pieces for different rooms. Naked: unconcealed, nothing hidden under the surface that would contradict what shows. Third, the questions keep coming. Will you ever, he asks, taste a loving and contented disposition? Be full, needing nothing, craving nothing, not wanting more time to enjoy pleasures, or a better place, or nicer weather, or better company? Will you be satisfied with what's here, and believe that all is well with you? Fourth, why this matters on a Tuesday. Some tiredness may not come from the work at all, but from the switching: managing the faces, minding the gap between the person inside and the one we're presenting. Marcus wants to close that gap. Not by telling everyone everything; simple doesn't mean blurting. It means there's one person in there, the same in every room. And notice how he asks: as a question, to himself, with no answer written down.
screen: `MY SOUL, WILL YOU EVER?` · `GOOD, SIMPLE, ONE, UNCONCEALED.` · `FULL, NEEDING NOTHING.` · `ONE PERSON IN EVERY ROOM.` · then, large: `SIMPLE AND WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of a room in your life where you wear the heaviest face: a meeting, a family visit, a feed. Picture what you hide there. Not secrets that belong to other people; just the parts of yourself you trim away. Ask: is there one small, true thing I could let show there? A real opinion, kindly said. A real feeling. A plain no. Choose one. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Contented disposition. Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever taste a loving and contented disposition, satisfied with what's here. Today's word.
Your line: simple and whole. Be unconcealed once today: let one true thing show, kindly, where you'd usually hide it. Day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations sometimes use Marcus's opening question in book ten as an honest self-check, asking where they present a different self in different rooms, and choosing one place to be plainer.

fork.setup: you're at a dinner where everyone expects you to agree with something you don't believe. you're Marcus, asking his soul to be simple and whole. what does that look like?
options: say what you really think, kindly and plainly.
announce every disagreement you've ever had.
fork.reveal: Marcus asks his soul to be simple and unconcealed: the same person in every room. that isn't blurting, just not hiding.

original.note: Greek: simple, single, one-fold. one of the things Marcus asks his soul to be.

trapdoor: what you thought: be a good person.
what it means: be one person, simple and unconcealed, the same in every room, and content with what's here.
what a scholar hears: haplous can mean single as well as simple, and is set against diplous, double; to be simple is not to be doubled.

notes: 10.1 paraphrased (Long: 'Wilt thou, then, my soul, never be good and simple and one and naked, more manifest than the body which surrounds thee? ... Wilt thou never be full and without a want of any kind, longing for nothing more...?'). Confirm details including 'better weather' (Long: 'more pleasant climate') and 'all is well with you'.
Confirm ἁπλοῦς appears in 10.1 and the haplous/diplous contrast.
